column4: The section's cloud over Ad's valleys is the cloud its people take for a rain-bearing one; the ayah corrects that expectation with “رِيحٌ فِيهَا عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ”.
The preceding cloud's punishment is realized here as a wind that “تُدَمِّرُ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ”; this supplies the destructive force behind the section's cloud-to-judgment meeting.

The section joins water descending in a flood with punishment; this flood account opens heaven's gates with pouring water, and 54:12 completes the scene with springs bursting from earth and the waters meeting.
The section's stated water sense of the root ف ج ر meets “فَجَّرْنَا الْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا”; the verse's springs rise from earth and meet the rain of 54:11, making the upper and lower waters one flood.

“لَمَّا طَغَى الْمَاءُ” names water overflowing its bounds, the section's flood image; here that deluge carries people in the ship, whereas the section's overflowing violence receives a lash of punishment.
This retelling names Aad's destruction by a violent, barren wind, a second account of the storm the section reads into the cloud over their valley.
The wind is sustained over Aad for seven nights and eight days; the next ayah records its aftermath, extending the section's brief cloud-to-destruction scene.
The wind's result is that no remnant of the people is seen; this is the outcome of the prolonged Ad storm described in 69:6 and 69:7.
The ayah describes winds raising and spreading clouds until rain emerges; it gives the merciful version of the cloud that Ad mistake for rain in the section's cited 46:24.
The people rejoice after having despaired before the rain; this neighboring response makes explicit the hope and reversal that the section contrasts with Ad's false expectation.
The rain leaves traces of mercy by reviving dead earth; this is the saving effect of the cloud in 30:48, opposite the destruction that arrives under Ad's cloud.
Winds are sent as glad tidings before mercy here, a direct reversal of the section's cloud that looks like rain but carries punishment.
The water from heaven gives life to dead land and drink to people and livestock; 25:48 introduces the merciful winds, contrasting Ad's cloud and punishment.
Winds drive heavy clouds and rain revives a dead land; this concrete rain-bearing cloud is the merciful counterpart to the cloud over Ad's valley.

The source section explicitly links the verb صَبَّ, a water-pouring action, to a lash of عَذَاب; this verse commands that boiling punishment be poured over a head, bringing water and torment together in its own scene.
The same root ص ب ب appears in “صَبَبْنَا الْمَاءَ صَبًّا” for poured rain; the next verses show it yielding food, the life-giving water action set against the section's poured punishment.

The section's word عَذَاب is paired in its prose with the sweet-water sense of ع ذ ب; this verse calls one of two seas “عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ”, making the hoped-for taste concrete beside the other, salty water.
This second water contrast names one sea “عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ” and the other bitter; it supports the section's explicit wordplay between عَذَاب and sweet water without confusing the two meanings.
The section's stated water sense of ف ج ر appears in “فَجَّرْنَا خِلَالَهُمَا نَهَرًا”: a river is made to flow through two gardens, joining its spring-water and garden images.
The section's garden and the secondary water sense of ف ج ر meet in “وَفَجَّرْنَا فِيهَا مِنَ الْعُيُونِ”, where springs are made to gush within gardens of palms and grapes.

The section explicitly names the water sense of ف ج ر; here Allah's servants drink from a spring and “يُفَجِّرُونَهَا تَفْجِيرًا”, directing its flow as they will, a blessed counterpart to the flood of punishment.
The section cites this verse's mountains scattered until the land is left level; its “صَفْصَفًا” is the same dictionary word the section derives from ص ف ف for a level plain.
The land is so level that no depression or elevation remains; this neighboring detail completes the plain produced by the scattered mountains in 20:106 and marks the boundary after upheaval.
The mountains are moved and earth appears level, while all people are gathered; this unites the section's flattened ground and the arrival of beings upon it.
On the Day of the Spirit and angels standing in ranks, the same rowed assembly arrives on a judgment scene, matching the section's angels lined across the leveled ground.
Hell is named “مِرْصَادًا”, an ambush or watchpoint; this is the same waiting-place image the section hears in its word for God's watch over the transgressors.
The next verse names the transgressors as Hell's destination; it specifies whom the ambush of 78:21 awaits, as the section connects watchfulness with punishment.
The opening oath names those who are ranged in rows; the section's repeated صفّ imagery likewise leaves angelic ranks standing after the built structures fall.

The source section names the dictionary sense “extended columns” (عَمَدٍ مُمَدَّدَةٍ); this verse uses that exact phrase for the confinement of the wealth-hoarder, joining its pillar image to his gathered wealth.
The person “الَّذِي جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ” piles up and counts wealth, the heap paired by the section with the upright columns of 104:9.
This person's belief that wealth will make him last forever completes the portrait begun in 104:2; it supports the section's claim that neither piling wealth nor erecting columns saves their owner.

When called to set out, people “اثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ” and prefer this world's life; the section uses this exact earth-clinging image as the contrary of the tranquil soul's return to its Lord.
People come to God singly, leaving their possessions behind and finding no intercessors; this is the section's solitary person without anyone to stand beside or support him.

After being told to enter the Garden, the slain believer wishes his people knew; his “يَا لَيْتَ قَوْمِي يَعْلَمُونَ” is an after-entry wish, unlike the section's regretful wish to have prepared beforehand.

The speaker says his Lord made him one of the honored after forgiving him; this neighboring ayah grounds the section's contrast between honor inferred from wealth and honor received through forgiveness.
At death the wrongdoer asks to be returned so he can act rightly; this is the unfulfilled return-wish opposite the section's soul welcomed back and already inside the Garden.
The requested return is refused and a barrier remains until resurrection; this completes 23:99 and sharpens the section's contrast with a return granted to the contented soul.
The God-fearing are brought to the Garden in groups; that communal entry answers the section's single orphan image with the soul entering among God's servants.
On orphans the verse says that mixing with them makes them “your brothers”; this gives concrete support to the section's image of honoring the lone orphan by joining and backing him.
The righteous give food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving it; this puts the section's orphan beside its table and turns support into a shared meal.
The difficult ascent is feeding someone on a day of hunger; 90:15 and 90:16 specify the orphan and destitute, completing the food scene that meets the section's orphan image.
The hungry person is an orphan close in kin; this places the orphan directly inside the feeding scene begun in 90:14 and continued in 90:16.
The next person named is one in misery and dust; together with 90:14 and 90:15 this completes the passage's concrete call to feed the vulnerable.
The denier of judgment repels the orphan, the opposite of the section's call to honor and draw near to him.
He does not encourage feeding the poor; this neighboring rebuke completes 107:2's treatment of the orphan and reverses the section's table and care images.
The verse forbids mixing good property with bad and consuming orphan wealth with one's own; it directly illuminates the section's image of swallowing another's inheritance into one's private heap.
Men and women each have an allotted share of what parents and kin leave; this is the division the section says is erased when inheritance is gulped down whole.
Those who consume orphan property unjustly are said to consume fire into their bellies; it gives the moral consequence of the inheritance-hoarding the section depicts.
This verse assigns inheritance portions to children and parents; its detailed shares continue 4:7's principle, the precise opposite of clearing an inheritance without division.
Spousal and sibling shares are assigned here, continuing the same legal division and clarifying the multiple claims erased by a single hoard.
The reward is gardens with God pleased with them and they pleased with Him; this closely matches the section's “رَاضِيَةً مَرْضِيَّةً” and its reciprocal return.
This verse joins God's pleasure with theirs to entry into gardens; the mutual honor comes from truth and divine approval, reversing the section's claim that wealth proves honor.
Hearts “تَطْمَئِنُّ” through remembrance of God; that related root and stated cause give a concrete parallel to the section's soul made calm after upheaval.
The righteous are rewarded for patience with a garden; this supplies the garden setting for the section's welcomed soul and the spring image of 76:6.
The garden's shade hangs close over its inhabitants and its fruit is made easy to reach; this gives a concrete canopy to the section's reading of the final word as tree-cover.
Adam and his spouse use leaves of the Garden as a covering; the ayah makes concrete the section's meeting of the Garden word with the cover of trees.

Wealth and children are called adornments of worldly life, while lasting good deeds are better; the verse supplies the boundary against reading abundance as the honor the section's wealthy person claims.
Qarun is introduced with treasures so heavy their keys burden a group; this is a vivid individual heap of wealth against the section's account of wealth-love.
The earth swallows Qarun and his house, showing that the wealth-laden figure is not held up by the ground or saved by his possessions.
Onlookers realize that God expands or restricts provision as He wills; this corrects the assumption that riches prove honor, completing Qarun's downfall in 28:81.
Competition in accumulating more distracts people; it directly parallels the section's image of loving wealth as an ever-growing heap.
The competition lasts until people visit the graves; this completes 102:1 and shows the limit of the accumulating that the section says cannot save.
Every person comes to God alone on the Day of Resurrection; this repeats the section's solitary arrival, while its other image offers entry among the servants as the answer to aloneness.
On the Day each person flees from his brother; the following verses extend the separation through parents, spouse, and children, giving social detail to the section's unsupported single arrival.
Flight from one's mother and father extends the separation begun in 80:34; the scene makes the absence of human backing concrete.
Flight from spouse and children continues the same Day-of-judgment separation, adding the closest household ties to the solitary scene.
Each person is occupied with his own concern; this completes the family-flight passage and explains the section's image of no one standing behind the solitary person.

In another account of Moses, water issues from a struck rock for twelve tribes; it repeats the section's meeting of a spring and a people, though this wording uses a different root from its named ف ج ر sense.

The disbelievers demand that the Prophet make a spring gush from earth (“تُفَجِّرَ لَنَا”); the same ف ج ر water sense is framed as a demand, unlike the spring assigned for the servants in the section's 76:6 link.
When Moses strikes the rock, twelve springs burst forth; “ٱنفَجَرَتْ” is the section's secondary water sense of ف ج ر, here supplying a people rather than a garden.
After the flood, earth is told to swallow its water and the sky to stop; the waters subside and the ark settles, a measured ending to the overflow named in the section.
Aad are punished by a cold, furious wind over days of misery; it is another account of the wind that turns the hoped-for cloud into destruction.
A barren wind is sent against Aad; this repeated account supports the destructive side of the section's rain-cloud encounter.
The wind leaves nothing it reaches without making it like decayed remains; this neighboring result completes 51:41's barren storm.
The earth is shaken with a mighty shaking on the final day, echoing the repeated crushing of earth in the section's judgment scene.
The mountains are crushed and pulverized; this follows the earthquake in 56:4 and develops the flattening of the judgment landscape.
The mountains become scattered dust, completing the land's upheaval in 56:4 and 56:5 before the section's aligned ranks appear.
Mountains are crushed with one crushing before the Day's event arrives; this places ruined terrain beside the advent that the section stages on a flattened plain.
The inevitable event occurs immediately after the crushed mountains of 69:14; the sequence parallels the section's placement of destruction and arrival on one ground.
The earth is violently shaken at the final hour; this repeats the upheaval that precedes the section's calm soul and assembly.
The earth brings its burdens out after the shaking; this continues 99:1's scene and gives the upheaval a visible result.
The sky's “سِرَاجًا وَهَّاجًا” is a blazing lamp, a concrete light-source parallel to the section's dictionary image of the dawn's standing column of light.
Abundant water is poured from the clouds; this follows the blazing lamp in 78:13 and joins the section's light, rain, and garden images.
The poured water brings grain and plants; this completes the provision begun in 78:14 and shows water becoming sustenance rather than punishment.
The same water sequence produces lush gardens; this neighboring culmination connects the section's cloud and garden meeting.
God is “فَالِقُ الْإِصْبَاحِ”, cleaving daybreak from night; it gives a direct parallel to the section's opening dawn breaking a covering of darkness.
Dawn is distinguished as the white thread from the black thread of night; this makes the section's image of dawn emerging through darkness concrete.
The oath “وَالصُّبْحِ إِذَا تَنَفَّسَ” pictures morning breathing; it extends the section's dawn as a force that opens darkness.
Day is sworn by as it reveals, paired with night that covers in 91:4; this mirrors the section's meeting of dawn breaking one cover and a garden as another.
Night is “إِذَا يَغْشَىٰهَا”, covering the day; its contrast with 91:3 sharpens the section's image of dawn splitting darkness.
The source section names فُجُور as moral violation; here “فُجُورَهَا” is paired with taqwa as the soul's contrary moral capacities, preserving the section's link between opening and transgression.
The root's moral form appears in the wish “لِيَفْجُرَ أَمَامَهُ”; the person wants to persist in wrongdoing, a specific instance of the section's fujur tearing through religious restraint.
The “فُجَّار” are placed in Hell; this uses the same moral word named by the section and connects transgression to its judgment landscape.
The Garden's food is lasting and its shade enduring; this supports the section's meeting of the Garden word with tree-cover, while the section's 76:6 link supplies the gushing spring.
The orphan is explicitly not to be oppressed; this is a direct moral reversal of abandoning the lone child whom the section says should be honored.
Qarun claims his fortune comes from his own knowledge; this self-grounding, answered by his downfall in 28:81, parallels the section's wealthy person reading possessions as proof of honor.
When a people forget the warning, they are given abundance before being seized suddenly; this is a specific reversal of treating plentiful provision as proof of divine favor.
Abraham asks for a sign of resurrection “لِيَطْمَئِنَّ قَلْبِي”; the related root gives a concrete parallel to the section's reassured soul at the threshold of the afterlife.

The verse uses the ambush form “مَرْصَدٍ” for those lying in wait on roads; it gives a human road-side instance of the section's ambush-word, while reversing the divine watcher into people waiting for opponents.
